name: Night Radio Call
blurb: A late-night radio host takes a call from a listener who sounds strangely familiar
title: Night Radio Call: 2-Person Voice Drama Script
description: A 4-minute audio drama for 2 voices of any gender: a late-night radio host takes a call from a listener who is not quite who they seem. Free to record.
h1: Night Radio Call: a 4-Minute Voice Drama Script for 2 Voices
logline: It is two in the morning and Jamie is hosting the quietest show on the radio. A caller on line three wants to dedicate a song to their child, who falls asleep to this station every night, and the more they talk, the less the details add up.
setting: A small radio studio at night, and a phone at the other end. For recording: two microphones or one, a desk, a mug, a sheet of paper.

roles.name: Host
roles.note: 30 to 45, any gender. Jamie, a calm late-night radio host. Good at listening, used to lonely callers.

roles.name: Caller
roles.note: 30 to 40, any gender. A warm, tired parent calling a radio show for the first time. Wants to leave something for their child.

script.sfx: A soft instrumental piano piece fades out. The low hum of a studio. A mug set down.

script.say: That's two o'clock. If you're awake, you're with me. This is Jamie, and this is the small hours. The lines are open. Line three, you're on the air.
script.how: close to the mic, low and warm

script.sfx: A faint crackle on the line, like an old phone.

script.say: Oh. Hello. Am I on? Sorry. I've never done this before.
script.how: on the phone, a little breathless

script.say: You're doing fine. What's your name?
I'd rather not, if that's all right. I'm only calling for a dedication.
That's all right. Who's it for?
My little one. They're six. They fall asleep to this station every night. Under the covers with the radio. They think I don't know.
I did that too, when I was a kid. Same station, actually.
Did you? That's nice. Then you know.
And where are you calling from tonight?
The phone box by the hospital. The one with the broken door. It's pouring out here.

script.sfx: Rain on glass, faint, only on the caller's line.

script.say: Is it? It's a dry night here.
Must be just this side of town.
A phone box. I didn't know there were any left.
There's one on every corner.
What's your little one like?
Serious. Asks questions about everything. Last week it was, where does the radio voice go when the radio is off? I said, home to bed, like everyone else.
That's a good answer.
They didn't believe me. They said the voice must live inside the radio. They want to be one, you know. A voice on the radio.
Do they.

script.action: A pause on the line. The host's chair creaks.

script.say: So why the hospital, if you don't mind me asking?
I'm a patient. Just for a bit. My chest. The nurses let me walk down when I can't sleep. My partner's at home with the little one. They tell them I'm working nights.
That's kind of them.
It's easier. Kids worry. Mine worries about everything. Leaves the hall light on. Counts the stairs.
Counts the stairs.
Thirteen. Every night. Out loud. Can I ask you something? You sound like a grown-up who turned out all right.
Some days.
Does it get better? Being a grown-up? I worry I won't see much of it. Theirs, I mean.

script.action: A long silence in the studio.

script.say: It gets better. They grow up fine. They get a bit stubborn. They still leave the hall light on.
You say that like you know them.
I think I might. Listen. What's the song you'd like?
Anything with a piano. They like the piano ones. Just say it's from the one who's working nights. They'll understand when they're older.
I'll say it. Is there anything else? Anything you want them to hear?
That I'm proud of them. That I'm sorry about the stairs. No, that's silly. Just say goodnight.
It's not silly.

script.sfx: The pips of a payphone running out of credit.

script.say: Oh, that's my money gone. Thank you, Jamie. That's a lovely name. It's my little one's name too.
Wait. Please. Just one more minute.

script.sfx: The line clicks. A long dial tone. Then nothing.

script.say: My producer's passed me a note. It says line three hasn't been connected since they changed the switchboard. Twenty-nine years ago.
script.how: after a long breath, back on air

script.say: Well. This next one is for a caller on line three. It's from the one who's working nights. And it goes out to a kid with the radio under the covers, who never stopped listening.
Goodnight.

script.sfx: A soft piano piece begins and slowly fills the room. Far away, very faint, rain.

ul: Record the two voices in different spaces if you can: the host close on a good microphone, the caller a little further back or through a phone filter, so the caller always sounds slightly far away.
Keep the rain only on the caller's line. That single sound detail is the first clue, so mix it quietly and never under the host.
Use plain sound for everything else: a mug on a desk, a chair creak, paper rustling. Royalty-free or self-made piano music works for the opening and closing; avoid songs with lyrics.
If you perform it live on stage, put the host at a desk with a lamp and the caller in a separate pool of light holding an old phone receiver, never looking at each other.
For a self-tape or class, one actor can read both parts with a phone filter on the caller, or two actors can sit back to back so neither sees the other's face.
The host starts in professional mode, smooth and gentle. Every detail that matches the host's childhood should chip a little of that polish away.
The caller never knows what is happening. Play them as entirely ordinary and warm; the eeriness comes from the host's reactions, not from a spooky voice.
Counts the stairs is the moment the host understands. Drop almost to a whisper and leave a gap before the caller continues.
The host must hold it together on air. The audience feels more when the host is trying not to cry than when the host cries.
Leave real silence before the producer's note. In audio, two or three seconds of nothing is huge.
Make it a voice message or a late-night podcast call-in instead of radio; the dropped line still works.
Make the caller a grandparent or an older sibling, and change the hospital to a night shift at a factory or a ship at sea.
Write a part two where the host, the next night, opens line three on purpose and waits.

prompts.keyframe: A small dim radio studio at 2 a.m., an adult host in headphones leaning close to a microphone, a desk lamp and a steaming mug, a window behind showing a dry city night, soft amber glow, cinematic still, 16:9.
shots: Close-up of a radio host speaking softly into a microphone, slow push-in, amber lamp light, calm late-night mood.
Medium shot of an adult in an old phone box at night, rain streaming down the glass, holding the receiver and smiling tiredly, gentle handheld sway, bittersweet mood.
Close-up on the host's face going very still while listening through headphones, eyes glistening, static camera, quiet eerie mood.
Wide shot of the empty studio as the host slides a note aside and leans back to the microphone, light dims slowly, bittersweet ending.

faq.q: Can I record Night Radio Call for a podcast or a monetised channel?
faq.a: Yes. It is an original voice drama under CC BY 4.0. Record it, post it and use it in competitions, and credit Script: cv.cm. Use your own or royalty-free music for the piano cues.
The script leaves it open. The caller is the host's parent, calling from the past through a line that no longer exists. Play it as gentle and bittersweet, not as horror.

faq.q: How do I make the caller sound like they are on a phone?
faq.a: Record the caller normally and add a telephone or band-pass filter in any free audio editor, or record the caller through a phone on speaker. Add light crackle at the start of the call.
